conversation.content: Today we're going to design a real-time chat system, like WhatsApp or Slack. Users should be able to send and receive messages instantly. What questions do you have?
Okay, so a chat system. How many users? And is this one-on-one or group chat too?
50 million DAU. Both one-on-one and group chats. Groups can have up to 500 members. Average user sends 40 messages per day. What else?
Do we need message history? And should messages be encrypted?
Yes to message history — users should see the last 30 days by default. No end-to-end encryption needed for now. Let's start designing. How would you approach the architecture?

Sure. So the user opens the app and wants to send a message. They'd make a REST API call, like POST /api/messages, with the recipient and message body. The server receives it, stores it in the database, and then the recipient can fetch it with GET /api/messages.
Interesting. With this approach, how does the recipient know a new message has arrived? When does the recipient call GET /api/messages?
The recipient's client could poll the server every few seconds. Like every 3 seconds, it calls GET /api/messages?since=last_timestamp to check for new messages.

With 50 million users polling every 3 seconds, that's about 17 million requests per second just for polling — and most of those return empty responses. Is there a more efficient way to push messages to clients in real-time?
Hmm, I guess we could reduce the polling frequency? Like every 10 seconds? Or maybe only poll when the app is in the foreground?

That reduces the load but the fundamental issue remains — the client is always asking 'any new messages?' Have you heard of WebSockets or long polling? These are techniques where the server can push data to the client.

Oh, right. WebSockets. I've heard of them but haven't used them. So the idea is the client opens a connection and the server can send messages to the client without the client asking? So it's like a two-way REST API?

Close — it's a persistent bidirectional connection. Unlike REST which is request-response, a WebSocket stays open and either side can send data at any time. How would you integrate this into your architecture?

Okay so... the client connects to the server with a WebSocket. When user A sends a message to user B, user A sends it over the WebSocket to the server. The server stores it and then... sends it to user B over user B's WebSocket connection. But what if user B is connected to a different server? I'd use a REST API call between the servers.

You've identified the right problem — user B might be on a different server. A REST call between servers could work but it means every server needs to know which server every user is connected to. What about using a message broker or pub/sub system to decouple this?

A message broker... like a queue? So server A puts the message in a queue and server B reads from the queue? But how does server B know to read it? Sorry, I'm not very familiar with message brokers. Could we just use a REST API instead? Each server exposes a /deliver endpoint and we look up which server the user is on from a database?

That database lookup adds latency on every message. Let me explain briefly — with pub/sub, each server subscribes to channels for its connected users. When a message comes for user B, it's published to user B's channel, and whichever server has that user gets the message automatically. But let's move on. How would you store messages?

I'd use MySQL. A messages table with columns: id, sender_id, recipient_id, content, timestamp. For group messages, I'd have a group_messages table with group_id instead of recipient_id. To get messages for a conversation, SELECT * FROM messages WHERE (sender_id = A AND recipient_id = B) OR (sender_id = B AND recipient_id = A) ORDER BY timestamp.
With 50 million users sending 40 messages each per day, that's 2 billion messages daily. How does a single MySQL instance handle that write load and table size?

I guess we'd need to add more MySQL servers? Like a master-slave setup? The master handles writes and the slaves handle reads. And we could partition the table by date, so each day's messages are in a separate partition.

Even with partitioning, a single master handling 2 billion writes per day — about 23,000 per second — would struggle. Have you considered sharding across multiple databases? Or using a database designed for high write throughput like Cassandra?

Sharding... we could split by user ID? So messages for users 1-1000000 go to shard 1, etc. But then for a conversation between two users on different shards, where does the message go? Maybe we shard by conversation ID instead?
Sharding by conversation ID is a reasonable approach. Let's talk about what happens when a user is offline. How do they get their messages when they come back online?

When they come back online, they'd make a REST API call to get all messages since they were last seen? Like GET /api/messages?since=last_seen_timestamp. The server queries the database for all messages after that timestamp.
That works for the initial sync. What about push notifications to wake up the app when a message arrives while offline?

Oh, push notifications. We'd use Apple's push notification service for iOS and Google's for Android. When a message comes in and the user is offline, instead of sending over WebSocket, we'd call the push notification API. I'm not sure about the implementation details though.
That's the right idea. We're running low on time. Is there anything else you'd add to the design?

I'd add read receipts — when user B reads a message, send an update back. And maybe typing indicators. And we'd need to handle the case where a message fails to deliver and needs to be retried. I realize I should know more about real-time systems. I'm more comfortable with standard request-response architectures.

I appreciate your honesty. You showed some good instincts around sharding and the offline sync problem. I'd recommend studying WebSockets, message brokers, and pub/sub patterns — they're core to many systems. Thank you for your time.

strengths: Honest about knowledge gaps rather than bluffing
Identified the cross-server delivery problem without prompting
Showed some improvement on sharding when guided toward conversation-based partitioning
weaknesses: Fundamental gap in real-time systems knowledge — defaulted to REST polling for everything
No capacity estimation performed at all
Never mentioned caching, CDNs, or any performance optimization
Could not bridge the gap from REST to event-driven architecture even with heavy guidance
No discussion of failure handling, message ordering, or delivery guarantees
